summary: Curtis Island Light guards the entrance to Camden Harbor: an 1836 light, a brick tower of 1896, automated in 1972, and now a town park.

access.note: A town park, reached by boat only; there is no dock. The grounds are open; the dwelling and tower are closed.

events.note: Galt's rubblestone tower and stone dwelling; USLHS gives 1835 as the establishment year
A February gale cracked the first tower; inspector I. W. P. Lewis reported it (per LighthouseFriends)
Fourth-order Fresnel lens; LighthouseFriends dates its use 1857 to 1994
Dwelling replaced by a framed house on the old foundation
New cylindrical brick tower replaced the rubblestone tower
Keeper's 14-year-old daughter rowed to two capsized boys near the island
Renamed from Negro Island to Curtis Island for Cyrus H. K. Curtis
Keeper plucked a pilot from the water after an Air Force T33 crashed (LighthouseFriends)
Coast Guard automation; the town took the island and buildings (except the tower)
Town of Camden took responsibility for the island and its buildings except the tower
Town accepted ownership of the tower under the Maine Lights Program (Nov. 1997)

corrections.current: tower, conical_masonry, brick, built 1835, 7.5 m, standing
corrections.proposed: tower, cylindrical_masonry, brick, built 1896, 7.6 m (25 ft), standing
corrections.why: The present tower is the cylindrical brick tower of 1896 (USLHS: CYLINDRICAL, 25 ft; LighthouseFriends). The first tower was rubblestone, built 1836, and was demolished in 1896.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The USLHS 1835 is the establishment year. The NRHP and LighthouseFriends give 1836 for the first tower, so the record's 1835 date for the tower is the archive's year, not the tower's.

notes_for_editor: Keepers come from the USLHS roster (NARA registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory), matched to the station by name and position; the rows are not yet confirmed in primary records. Contractors (Oliver A. Andrews, George Galt) are not keepers and are not in the roster; Galt is named in the prose. Dates disagree: the USLHS place record gives 1835 as the establishment year; the NRHP and LighthouseFriends give 1836 for the first tower. The NRHP scan reads the builder's name as 'Galilt'; LighthouseFriends and the USLHS roster read 'Galt'. The Light-House Board's FY1896 report already lists the tower, workroom and covered way as rebuilt, while its FY1897 report puts the move into the new tower on 31 July 1896 and LighthouseFriends gives 30 July. Scan pages checked 2026-10-22 with corpus.py page: FY1894 p.349, FY1895 p.226, FY1896 pp.36 and 51 (the torkroom line is on p.51), FY1897 pp.265, 269 and 293, FY1900 p.49, FY1901 p.71. Board page numbers are scan pages from the Internet Archive; printed page numbers were not confirmed. The FY1896 report (year to 30 June 1896) lists the tower as rebuilt before either July date; the FY1897 report gives 31 July 1896 for the lantern's move. The story states that disagreement. LighthouseFriends is the only source for the 1842 gale, the 1856 lens, the 1962 rescue, the 1970 transfer, the Brown death and the name origin. The record's characteristic (Oc G 4s) and range (6 nm) are not in any source read here, so they are not in facts. The record's NRHP listing date (1973) was not checked against the nomination form. The archive lists the station as not open to the public (Open to Public: No); LighthouseFriends says the grounds are open and the dwelling and tower closed. The story gives both. A tourism listing seen in search gives 1998 for the town's ownership of the tower, against the November 1997 vote that LighthouseFriends reports; the listing was not read in full and is not used. Page images were not viewed; each Board entry was read from the cached OCR text around it (corpus.py page). The FY1896 'workroom' reading rests on the OCR word 'torkroom' (scan p.51) and is marked in the story's footnote. The Fort Point and Grindel fog-bell and boundary lines were checked the same way.
